title: Hanukkah: giving
hookLine: coins for children, and giving to those in need
tomorrow: why go hungry for a siege that ended long ago?

cards: Gold foil with chocolate inside, a spinning top, and a pile of coins changing hands all evening. That's gelt, Yiddish for money: the coins of Hanukkah, often for children.

Under the chocolate sits an old question the Talmud actually argues out. Someone has only enough money for one: oil for the Hanukkah lamp, or wine for Kiddush, the blessing that opens the Sabbath. Which one wins?

teach.b: The sage Rava raises it himself, and gives both sides a voice. For Kiddush: it comes every single week, and what comes often has the first claim.

teach.h: HANUKKAH: IT MAKES THE MIRACLE KNOWN.
teach.b: For the Hanukkah lamp: it makes the miracle known; it speaks to the whole street. Then he decides: the Hanukkah lamp, for making the miracle known. But there's a second pair.
The Hanukkah lamp, or the ordinary lamp that lights the home on the Sabbath?

teach.h: PEACE IN THE HOUSE COMES FIRST.
teach.b: The home lamp wins, for peace in the house. A dark, tense home comes first.
So the Talmud weighs light by what it does: peace inside first, then the light that tells the miracle outside, then the weekly blessing. Maimonides adds a line that changes what coins are for.
Even someone who lives on charity, he says, should borrow, or sell a garment, to buy oil and light. Which means someone has to give.
That's the second life of gelt: not only chocolate for the kids, but money so another family's window is lit too.
Some families do both: coins to play with, and coins to give away.

how: At Hanukkah, families give children gelt, real coins or chocolate ones, often used to play dreidel; some also give tzedakah during the eight days, so others can light and celebrate too.

games.q: two families on your street: one can afford candles and not much else, the other can't afford candles at all. you've got a few dollars of gelt. what does Maimonides' line point to?
o: buy more candles for your own window.
help the family without candles light theirs.
keep it; gelt is a gift for you, not to pass on.
games.why: Maimonides says even someone living on charity should light. that only works if someone gives.

practice: For the sit, hold a coin if you have one, or imagine its weight in your palm. Think of two places it could go: a treat for someone you love, or a gift to someone who's short this winter.
You don't have to choose now; just notice which one makes the coin feel lighter.
